common_name: Green German Sugarcane (Heirloom Gulf South Syrup Cane)

planting.note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Green German is a traditional Gulf South dooryard syrup cane named by University of Florida IFAS Extension among the low-sucrose canes preferred for kettle syrup over crystal sugar.

directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Green German is an old dooryard heirloom, unstriped and solid deep green-stalked, that UF/IFAS Extension lists alongside Louisiana Ribbon as one of the traditional syrup-type canes: its juice carries a lower sucrose-to-total-sugars ratio than crystal (refining-grade) cane, which resists graining up in the kettle and cooks down into a smooth, pourable table syrup rather than crystallized sugar. Because sugarcane rarely sets viable seed true-to-type in Gulf South conditions, growers propagate it entirely from stalk sets: in fall, before the first hard freeze, the healthiest, disease-free stalks are cut, laid horizontally in a shaded trench or covered cane bed, and mulched heavily with soil, pine straw, or plastic sheeting to keep them dormant but unfrozen through winter. Harvest for syrup runs from the first light frosts in late October through December, when cool nights have converted starches to sugar; stalks are stripped of leaves, crushed, and the juice slow-cooked in an open kettle or pan evaporator into dark, mild-flavored cane syrup.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Backyard Sugarcane (SS-AGR-253/SC052)

common_name: Georgia Red Sugarcane (Heirloom Red-Stalked Chewing Cane)

planting.note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Georgia Red is a traditional all-red dooryard chewing cane named by University of Florida IFAS Extension alongside Yellow Gal among the region's heirloom chewing-type canes.

directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Georgia Red is an heirloom chewing cane with deep red to maroon, slender stalks, softer-rinded and juicier than syrup types, whose fibers stick together in a wad rather than shredding apart when chewed — the trait that defines a true chewing cane. It was traditionally bundled and sold fresh at farm stands, country stores, and gas stations across Georgia and the Gulf South each fall as a hand-peeled snack, gnawed in short sections for the sweet juice, though the stalks can also be pressed or cooked into syrup like any other cane. Propagate from stalk sets saved over winter: cut healthy stalks before hard frost, bed them in a shaded, well-drained trench under a heavy mulch of soil or pine straw to keep them dormant without freezing, and replant the sets in spring once the soil has warmed. Harvest for fresh eating can begin once stalks reach full size in September, but flavor and sweetness improve markedly after the first cool nights of fall concentrate the sugars in the stalk.

common_name: Home Green Sugarcane (Georgia Green Heirloom Dooryard Cane)

planting.note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Home Green (also called Georgia Green or Homeowner Green) is a dual-purpose heirloom dooryard cane grown for both chewing and syrup.

directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Home Green is a long-grown Gulf South dooryard heirloom, green-stalked through summer and ripening to a golden yellow with red-blushed, sunset-like mottling as stalks mature in fall; the rind is soft and easy to peel, the juice notably greener than most other heirloom canes, and growers describe the flavor as a simple, syrupy sweetness reminiscent of old-fashioned cane syrup. It is valued as a dual-purpose variety, equally suited to fresh chewing and to pressing and cooking down into syrup, and was traditionally kept in home dooryard patches rather than grown commercially. As with other heirloom canes, propagation is entirely from saved stalk sets: healthy stalks are cut before the first hard freeze, bedded horizontally in a shaded, well-drained trench, and covered with soil, pine straw, or plastic to hold them dormant through winter without freezing, then replanted the following spring. Harvest runs from the first light frosts of late fall, after cool nights have sweetened the stalks, through early winter.

common_name: White Transparent Sugarcane (Heirloom Pale-Stalked Chewing Cane)

planting.note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. White Transparent is a pale-stalked heirloom chewing cane preserved in the small dooryard-cane collections maintained in Florida and Louisiana.

directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. White Transparent is an old chewing-cane heirloom with pale, whitish-yellow-green stalks, distinct from the purple, red, and striped canes traditionally grown alongside it in the same dooryard patch. Like other chewing types it has a soft rind and high juice content, with fibers that cling together in a wad rather than shredding when gnawed, making it a favorite for fresh peeling and eating rather than crushing for syrup, though the juice can be pressed like any cane. It is maintained today mainly through small heirloom cane collections and informal seed-saver networks in Florida and Louisiana rather than commercial nurseries. Propagate from stalk sets saved over winter: cut healthy, disease-free stalks before the first hard freeze, bed them horizontally in a shaded, well-drained trench, and cover heavily with soil, pine straw, or plastic to keep them dormant without freezing until replanting the following spring once soil has warmed. Harvest for fresh chewing from October through December after cool nights have sweetened the stalks.
